question: SQ-LIP-000035
text: Do hormonal factors (puberty, pregnancy, menopause, estrogen) trigger or influence lipedema onset?
minor_problems: [minor] set: No proposition states that evidence for hormonal triggering is observational, retrospective and largely review- or consensus-based, with no prospective or causal data; the set may read as stronger than it is.
[minor] set: Reviews disagree on the direction of the ERalpha/ERbeta shift (E10, E25 vs E20, E27), which P3 hides under a neutral phrase.
[minor] set: Massive weight loss as a trigger (E11, 22%) is not represented in any proposition.

[minor] P1: two ideas; misplaced ['E12'] — suggested: Lipedema onset or worsening is frequently reported at female hormonal transitions, especially puberty, and also pregnancy and menopause, mostly by retrospective self-report. (Well supported descriptively, but evidence is recall-based, with consensus and reviews counted alongside surveys. E12 is a mechanistic male case proposal and belongs under P3, not onset timing. Bundles onset and worsening.)

[minor] P3: two ideas — suggested: Altered estrogen signalling in affected adipose tissue, including an altered estrogen receptor pattern and local aromatase activity, is proposed as a lipedema mechanism. (Almost entirely review-level proposals. Receptor direction is inconsistent across items (E10, E25 reduced ERalpha/increased ERbeta; E20, E27 increased ERalpha/ERbeta ratio), so 'imbalanced pattern' is the safe wording. E5 and E4 are one systematic review and do not address receptors or aromatase.)

[minor] P4: not fully supported; overgeneralized; two ideas — suggested: Some genetic findings in lipedema, including a familial AKR1C1 variant, involve hormone-related pathways, though evidence is sparse. ('Notably steroid hormone metabolism' rests on one family (E26, with reviews E24, E13, E15 echoing it) and a suggestive GWAS (E19). E21's quote shows 18 loci and heritability; the hormone-related correlations in the finding are not visible in the quote. Genetic links do not show that hormones trigger onset.)

propositions.statement: Circulating testosterone and estradiol are reported not to differ between women with lipedema and controls, though evidence is limited.
propositions.rationale: Systemic hormone measurements qualify hormonal hypotheses on a different axis from onset timing.

evidence.finding: Systematic review of lipedema pathology found no significant plasma differences in testosterone and estradiol versus controls; etiology remains largely uncertain.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Circulating estradiol and testosterone levels in lipedema may not differ from those of controls.

dropped.reason: Off-topic: mentions menopausal status only for cardiometabolic risk assessment; does not address hormonal triggers of lipedema onset.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Lipedema onset or worsening is frequently reported at female hormonal transitions, especially puberty, and also pregnancy and menopause, mostly by retrospective self-report.
verdicts.note: Well supported descriptively, but evidence is recall-based, with consensus and reviews counted alongside surveys. E12 is a mechanistic male case proposal and belongs under P3, not onset timing. Bundles onset and worsening.
Appropriately hedged ('reported by some women'); E3 is cross-sectional and E28 a single case, so no causal claim is made.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Altered estrogen signalling in affected adipose tissue, including an altered estrogen receptor pattern and local aromatase activity, is proposed as a lipedema mechanism.
verdicts.note: Almost entirely review-level proposals. Receptor direction is inconsistent across items (E10, E25 reduced ERalpha/increased ERbeta; E20, E27 increased ERalpha/ERbeta ratio), so 'imbalanced pattern' is the safe wording. E5 and E4 are one systematic review and do not address receptors or aromatase.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Some genetic findings in lipedema, including a familial AKR1C1 variant, involve hormone-related pathways, though evidence is sparse.
verdicts.note: 'Notably steroid hormone metabolism' rests on one family (E26, with reviews E24, E13, E15 echoing it) and a suggestive GWAS (E19). E21's quote shows 18 loci and heritability; the hormone-related correlations in the finding are not visible in the quote. Genetic links do not show that hormones trigger onset.
Hedged with 'may'; single systematic review. Consistent with a local rather than circulating hormonal mechanism, so not a contradiction of P3.

set_issues.issue: No proposition states that evidence for hormonal triggering is observational, retrospective and largely review- or consensus-based, with no prospective or causal data; the set may read as stronger than it is.
Reviews disagree on the direction of the ERalpha/ERbeta shift (E10, E25 vs E20, E27), which P3 hides under a neutral phrase.
Massive weight loss as a trigger (E11, 22%) is not represented in any proposition.
